turn_text: AgriPulse Open Mike is brought to you by the U.S. Grains Council. In tough economic times, it's good to remember that agriculture is one of America's bright spots. That's true at home, and it's true internationally. The United States is the world's top agricultural exporter with over 135 billion in exports last year. Those exports supported more than one million jobs at home. The U.S. Grains Council is one of the leaders of the U.S. AG-X4 team. It operates in over 50 countries to develop markets for U.S. corn, sorghum, barley, and co-products. Winning those markets is a team effort. The council partners with the USDA's foreign agricultural service to get the job done. That partnership, by the way, is just one more of the many programs that depend on the reauthorization of the Farm Bill. And now, agri-pulse open mike. Congressman Hugo Bauer, welcome to AgriPulse Open Mike.

turn_text: Well, Ken, thank you for having me on the program.
You have just finished the vote in the House of Representatives that passed a farm bill in a form that's never been passed before. What's your reaction to doing it this way?

Well, you know, obviously he was historic, you know, to divide the commodity title from the nutrition title. We've been having that discussion, you know, the last couple of farm bills, people wondered if you could do that. So we went down some uncharted waters today and passed the commodity title without the nutrition title. And after a disappointing vote a couple of weeks ago, it was nice to, I guess, move the ball down the field a little bit.

The chairman indicates this is an extreme move that he was not in favor of, but he's so in favor of getting a farm bill passed and getting a farm bill finished that he was willing to take this path. Do you want to respond to your chairman and the leadership he gave to getting this accomplished after the last bill failed?

Absolutely. Chairman Lucas has worked tirelessly to get our work done. As he said on the floor today, you know, our job here is to come and get the people's work done. And agricultural policy is extremely important to our country. It's important to our producers. And, you know, sometimes people would, after what happened two weeks ago, have given up, but Chairman Lucas was determined that we're going to get a five-year farm bill. He went to the leadership and said, let's figure out a way to look at this in a different way and find out how we can get more of our colleagues interested in voting for this. And so I come in him for doing that. You know, times have changed. Each farm bill that's done every five years is a different environment. And this is a different environment than the farm bill we did five years ago. And this is a different environment than the farm bill that was done 10 years ago. And so, just like in any other kind of business, you have to go with the conditions that you have. And while this is an extreme measure, today we had a little bit of success.

turn_text: What was the reasoning you had for agreeing to split the farm and the food and nutrition parts apart in this bill?

Well, if it would advance the Vince, the ball, I was for that because I've really felt like all along, the tradition is is that once you get the farm bill to a conference or once you can get the House and Senate to agree on a version each, that's really where, you know, you begin to make the most progress. But without the House having something to offer the Senate, you know, we really would be at a stalemate. And so in order to have something to go now to the Senate and talk about we needed a vehicle to do that and if we were able to do that by passing the commodity title first then you know I think that was a good strategy.

There are people who now say that Congress eats poison pills for breakfast and that all the things that have been set up in the past to make you pass legislation no longer are effective. And one of those was the permanent farm legislation that you repealed today. Do you agree?

Well, I think that's been somewhat in the past. I'm not sure that's a good policy for the American people. But what I do understand today is that basically what we had done with previous farm bills is extend the 49 act. And so what we did today is that the new permanent law will be this farm bill if and when it's passed and signed by the president. You can make You know, cases that that's a good or a bad thing, but what I would tell you is that I think this is a very good piece of legislation and that it's much more workable if in the future that we had to extend this policy rather than, you know, going back to the 49 Act, which actually is something that you couldn't actually implement. So you go from a poison pill maybe to a piece of permanent legislation that may be very favorable for production agriculture.
Are you concerned that if I'm correct there wasn't one single Democratic vote for this bill?

No, I think we expected that. That's the reason we spent basically all of this week talking to our Republican colleagues because we knew that if we were going to pass this bill that we were going to have to do it with Republican votes And we anticipated that the Democrats were not going to support us on that and they didn't disappoint us.

Congressman Nugabar, let me turn to the next step, which appears to be the conference. You're going in with just a portion of a bill with the Senate having a full bill. Doesn't that place you in an inferior position in the conference?

Well, not really because, you know, basically we'll see what the Senate has to offer and, you know, and how bad that they feel we need to move this ball down the road. And so I don't, you know, it's kind of hard to look in the crystal ball and determine, you know, what the ultimate outcome of this is going to be is I said that this was a, I felt like this was a first down, but it was not a touchdown today. And so, but we have advanced the ball, and so now the next play is, you know, it's beginning some informal discussion with the Senate before we really get into any kind of formal conference, because if it looks like they're not going to play ball, then we'll have to kind of assess, you know, where we go from here.
Well, now, if you were on that conference committee, what is your terminology of playing ball that they've got to go past their numbers on cuts in SNAP programs?

Well, I think at this particular point in time, I would just probably, you know, let's negotiate a commodity title. You know, they've passed a commodity title. We've commenced a commodity title. Let's see if we can agree on those numbers. And then, you know, come to an agreement on that, take those back to each chamber and send them to the president for his signature. And then I think what we'll have to do over in the House is determine, you know, what is a snap number that we can get passed in the House of Representatives. And, you know, and you take that back to the Senate and you try to work that out. What you understand, though, is the SNAP program, the FARM program expires on September 30th. The SNAP program is on autopilot, and so it will continue as current law until revised. And so there's probably less pressure on doing anything with the SNAP program than there is with the commodity title, because the commodity title on September 30th, you know, it terminates.
